Methods: Adults with suspected CNS infection at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo were enrolled.
After participants or their family members provided informed consent, approximately 0.5 -2 mL of leftover CSF was collected and stored at -80°C after all ordered clinical testing was in process.

Participants were excluded if less than 500µL of surplus CSF was available, CSF was stored at 4°C for greater than 48 hours before transfer to -80°C, medical records were unavailable for review, or antibiotics were administered for 7 or more days prior to lumbar puncture.

Sequencing data were processed via the open-source, cloudbased metagenomics platform, CZID, 20 and pathogen calls were determined via a previously published methodology. 18 A subset of participants had more than one aliquot of surplus CSF.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: The epidemiology of central nervous system (CNS) infections in low-and middle-income countries is poorly characterized due to limited access to specialized neurodiagnostic testing.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) can detect any pathogen in a single hypothesis-free assay but has largely been confined to high-income countries due to cost and infrastructure requirements.
We piloted an in-country CSF mNGS protocol in Lima, Peru to assess the feasibility of this approach in a resource-limited setting.
Methods: Adults with suspected CNS infection at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo were enrolled.
CSF mNGS (DNA and RNA) was performed in-country on a benchtop sequencer with half-volume library reactions and cloud-based analysis (CZID).
Paired sequencing at a significantly higher depth was performed on a subset of samples in the United States for validation.
Results: Among 43 participants (median age 48 years; 21% living with HIV), in-country mNGS detected 20 pathogens in 18 samples (42%), of which 65% were not identified by routine clinical testing.
Nine of 15 patients treated empirically for tuberculous meningitis were found to have a non-mycobacterial infection.
Detected organisms included Toxoplasma gondii, Taenia solium, Treponema pallidum, herpesviruses, and, on deeper sequencing, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus.
Deep sequencing recovered four pathogens missed at shallower-depth.
Conclusions: In-country CSF mNGS was feasible in Lima, Peru and recovered a clinically and epidemiologically meaningful spectrum of CNS pathogens, most missed by routine testing.
By utilizing available, lower-output sequencers, we overcame a principal barrier to deploying this technology where the burden of undiagnosed CNS infection is greatest.
Central nervous system (CNS) infections are commonly encountered in clinical practice in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Peru.

The epidemiology of these illnesses is poorly characterized due to the wide range of endemic pathogens, a significant immunosuppressed population that is at risk for unusual and opportunistic infections, and limited access to specialized neurodiagnostic testing.

HIV-associated opportunistic infectious diseases such as tuberculous meningitis (TBM), cerebral toxoplasmosis, and cryptococcal meningitis account for a significant portion of cases, in addition to neurocysticercosis, neonatal bacterial meningitis, and enteroviral and arboviral meningoencephalitis. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] The poor sensitivity of frontline diagnostic tests for TBM, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) GeneXpert, pose a particular clinical challenge, given the widespread prevalence of TB in urban Peru. [7] [8] [9] Since molecular and serologic CSF testing is limited, patients with subacute meningitis who test negative on CSF GeneXpert are often still thought to have TBM and empirically treated as such.

text.text: CSF metagenomic next generation sequencing (mNGS) is an increasingly important diagnostic tool in high-income settings, and several studies have demonstrated the utility of mNGS as a research-based tool to better understand the epidemiology of CNS infections in LMICs. 11, 12 By broadly amplifying and sequencing the nucleic acid present in a CSF sample, mNGS can theoretically identify any pathogen present, including unexpected and divergent organisms, without requiring an a priori hypothesis about the causative pathogen.

text.text: There were 9 participants (21%) living with HIV with a median CD4 count of 24 cells/mm 3 (range: 17-979) and a median viral load of 13,300 copies/mL (range: undetectable -157,000).
Six participants living with HIV were diagnosed during this same admission.
Most patients (n=36, 84%) had no neurologic symptoms or no significant disability (mRS 0-1) prior to the onset of current symptoms.
The most common presenting symptoms were headache (n=39, 91%), altered mental status (n=33, 77%), and neck stiffness (n=22, 51%).

CSF analysis commonly demonstrated mild pleocytosis (median=10 cells/mm 3 , IQR: 3-88 cells/mm 3 ), normal glucose (median=49 mg/dL, IQR: 40-58 mg/dL), and elevated protein (median=116 mg/dL, IQR 88-292 mg/dL).
The median length of hospital admission was 25 days (IQR 13-54.5), and median duration of follow up from the time of admission was 148 days (IQR: 41-383).
Three participants (7%) died during the hospitalization, and 8 (18.6%) had died during the follow up period.
Eleven participants required intubation (25.6%), and 8 (18.6%) required CSF diversion via either external ventricular drainage or ventriculoperitoneal shunting.

Nearly all participants experienced a worsening in their functional status at the time of discharge compared to their premorbid baseline (Figure 3D). mNGS results: CSF mNGS was performed in Peru to a median depth of 28M DNA reads (IQR: 18M -38M) and 12M RNA reads (IQR: 10M -13M).

Among pathogens detected via shallow-depth mNGS, 13 (65%) were not detected on routine clinical testing during the hospital admission.

Within the limitations of the available clinical data, the positive detections correlated with the clinical presentation with the exception of two cases of HTLV-1, which were felt to be incidental detections in the setting of blood contamination rather than the cause of the neurologic presentation (Supplemental Appendix).

Surplus CSF was available for 30 patients for deep sequencing at UCSF, which was performed to a median depth of 113M DNA reads (IQR: 39M -150M) and 151M RNA reads (IQR: 75M -155M).

After quality filtering and de-duplication, the average number of DNA and RNA reads was 3.7 and 6.9 times greater, respectively with deep sequencing compared to shallow-depth sequencing (p < 0.001, Figure 3C).

text.text: Pathogens were detected in 47% of samples with deep sequencing, including 4 that were missed on shallow-depth sequencing: Cryptococcus neoformans, M. tuberculosis, HSV-1, and an uncommon pathogen, the mosquito-borne alphavirus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV).
Two pathogens that were detected on shallow-depth sequencing were missed on deep sequencing, T. pallidum and T. gondii.

Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus: A man aged 71-75 years with angiosarcoma of the liver who had undergone surgical resection six months prior presented with three days of fever and one day of disorientation and word-finding difficulty after recently returning from the Peruvian Amazon.
CSF was notable only for an elevated protein of 115 mg/dL, with a normal cell count and glucose.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was not obtained.
The working diagnosis was metabolic encephalopathy, given his history of liver cancer, and the lactulose dose was increased.
He was discharged 7 days later with minimal change in his mental status.

While no pathogens were identified on shallow-depth sequencing, deep sequencing identified 794 RNA reads mapping to one region of the VEEV genome, spanning a contiguous region of approximately 190 base pairs within the nsP1-nsP2 replicase junction (genome positions 1930-2120); BLASTN analysis confirmed that all matching reads aligned exclusively to VEEV reference sequences, with no significant similarity to other alphavirus species.

T. gondii: A man aged 51-55 years with a recent diagnosis of pulmonary TB, on treatment, presented with three months of cough, weight loss, and constitutional symptoms, one month of headache and neck stiffness, and one day of being unable to answer basic questions.
He was newly diagnosed with HIV on admission (viral load and CD4 count unknown).
CSF showed 5 WBC/µL, a protein of 228 mg/dL, and a glucose of 39 mg/dL.
Neuroimaging revealed an isolated ring-enhancing lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere (Figure 4a).

Shallow-depth sequencing detected T. gondii, which uncommonly presents as an isolated lesion in the infratentorium (surplus CSF was not available for confirmatory deep sequencing).
A man aged 31-35 years presented with several weeks of headache and lower-extremity weakness and sensory loss.
CSF showed 2 WBC/µL and a protein of 129 mg/dL.
Spinal MRI demonstrated foci of hyperintense T2 signal within the thoracic cord with post-contrast enhancement (Figure 4b).

text.text: He was treated with plasmapheresis and corticosteroids without improvement and discharged wheelchair-dependent 30 days later.
Subsequent shallow-depth sequencing detected both T. pallidum and HTLV-1; both pathogens were confirmed on deep sequencing as well.

Syphilitic myelitis is a rare manifestation of neurosyphilis (on the order of ~1.5% of cases) and characteristically produces longitudinally extensive T2 signal with superficial, peripheral cord enhancement, the pattern seen here.

HTLV-1associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), by contrast, is generally (but not always) a chronic progressive myelopathy whose hallmark is cord atrophy rather than T2 signal hyperintensity or enhancement.

Therefore, the acute, swollen, and enhancing long-segment lesion was felt to be most likely due to the syphilitic process, with HTLV-1 regarded as a concurrent (and possibly chronic and contributory) infection rather than the driver of the acute presentation.
T. solium: A man aged 51-55 years without significant past medical history presented with two weeks of nausea, vomiting, headache, and one day of somnolence requiring noxious stimulation to arouse.
On presentation, testing demonstrated a mild peripheral leukocytosis (11.5 × 10⁹/L) and CSF with 30 WBC/µL (6% neutrophils, 94% mononuclear cells), a protein of 269 mg/dL, and a glucose of 24 mg/dL.
MRI demonstrated hydrocephalus with basal meningeal enhancement with cyst-like structures, most suggestive of racemose neurocysticercosis (Figure 4c).

Shallow-depth sequencing detected T. solium with numerous aligned reads, confirming the diagnosis.
In this study we show that CSF mNGS can be performed locally to reveal a clinically and epidemiologically meaningful spectrum of CNS pathogens in Lima, Peru.

Across 43 samples, mNGS performed locally detected at least one plausible pathogen in 42% of samples, and the majority of these organisms had not been identified by routine clinical testing performed during the admission.

The detections spanned DNA and RNA viruses, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, C. neoformans, and organisms that are difficult to diagnose with conventional assays: T. pallidum, Taenia solium, and Toxoplasma gondii.

CSF mNGS is established as a diagnostic capable of detecting a broad range of pathogens, and a recent single-center study demonstrated that approximately 20% of patients with CNS infections at a U.S. tertiary medical center were diagnosed via mNGS alone, underscoring the importance of this approach even in resource-rich settings. [21] [22] [23] Our findings extend that premise in two directions that matter for the settings where the diagnostic need is greatest: the sequencing was performed locally rather than sent to a reference center abroad, and it was performed at a depth low enough to allow for sequencing to be batched and performed on less costly and available equipment.

text.text: Samples were sequenced to a median of approximately 28 million DNA and 12 million RNA reads, roughly 3.7-fold and 6.9-fold fewer de-duplicated reads than the paired deep-sequencing runs performed on the validation subset. mNGS at a sequencing depth that is more practical in Peru allows for the assay to be run on low-output benchtop sequencers such as the iSeq, MiSeq, or NextSeq at an order-of-magnitude lower acquisition cost, a substantially smaller instrument footprint, and far lower service, maintenance, and reagent-commitment burdens than high-output platforms such as NovaSeq and similar platforms.
The capital expense and the ongoing service contracts of high-output sequencers are a primary reason clinical mNGS has remained concentrated in well-resourced reference laboratories.

This accessibility comes at a cost of sensitivity -on the paired validation subset, deeper sequencing recovered four pathogens that shallower sequencing did not (C. neoformans, M. tuberculosis, HSV-1 and VEEV).

The organisms missed at shallower depth were, as expected, those present at low genomic abundance in CSF, and laboratory validation and large prospective series of CSF mNGS have similarly shown that detection at the limit of the assay is governed by pathogen read abundance and input quality. 22, 24 Therefore, shallower-depth mNGS is best understood not as a replacement for deeper sequencing where maximal sensitivity is optimized, but as a high-throughput, lower-cost screening modality that trades low-end sensitivity for the accessibility that allows the assay to be operated locally.

text.text: An important limitation of CSF mNGS is highlighted by two detections, T. pallidum and T. gondii (both in participants distinct from the cases above), which were made on shallower-depth sequencing but not recovered on subsequent deeper sequencing of separate CSF aliquots.

Rather than indicating false-positive calls, this discordance likely represents the stochasticity of detecting low-abundance targets from limited nucleic-acid input, compounded by aliquot-to-aliquot variation.

This observation tempers the expectation that greater depth uniformly improves sensitivity, and underscores pre-analytic factors such as input volume, aliquoting, and low pathogen burden as primary determinants of detection at the low end. 25 Prior applications of CSF mNGS in low-and middle-income settings, including the characterization of neurological infection among people living with HIV in Peru, have reported that unbiased sequencing identifies a pathogen in a substantial fraction, approaching half of otherwise-undiagnosed cases. 5 Our positive-detection rate (42%) is concordant with that experience, and the ability to mirror this yield with a lower-resource workflow strengthens the validity of in-country CSF mNGS.

text.text: The clinical relevance of these detections is best illustrated by the subset of patients treated empirically for TBM.
Of 15 patients who were managed as presumptive TBM, mNGS identified a non-mycobacterial infection in nine.

This pattern reflects a recognized diagnostic difficulty -frontline molecular testing for TBM, including Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF, is insensitive, missing a substantial proportion of true cases, 7, 8, 26 so that a negative result cannot exclude TBM, and patients are frequently continued on empiric, monthslong anti-TB treatment in the absence of a confirmed diagnosis.

text.text: In addition to sequencing at a shallower-depth, several deliberate choices made the workflow feasible and affordable in this setting, and together they constitute a template that could be reproduced in a variety of settings.
Library preparation reactions utilized half the standard reagent volumes, reducing per-sample consumable costs.
Sequence analysis used a cloud-based pipeline (CZID), 20 which obviated the need for local highperformance computing infrastructure and specialized bioinformatics staff.

text.text: Several limitations should be emphasized.

CSF mNGS was performed months after each patient's admission as a retrospective research assay and thus, it did not inform real-time clinical management, and all statements of clinical impact are therefore necessarily conditional.
The results indicate how unbiased sequencing could have impacted clinical care had the results been available prospectively, not that it did contribute.
Second, the sample size is modest (n=43), and the cohort was assembled from residual CSF among consenting participants, introducing selection effects that limit epidemiologic generalization.

Third, CSF was banked and aliquoted before testing, and pre-analytic factors, such as input volume, freeze-thaw, and low pathogen burden, are expected to contribute to lower sensitivity, as reflected in the shallower-versus-deeper discordance discussed above. 25 Fourth, orthogonal confirmation was incomplete for some detections, and mNGS identification of one organism may not exclude concurrent infection.

text.text: Establishing actual clinical impact ultimately requires prospective, real-time deployment with formal measurement of turnaround time and effects on clinical decision-making.

We note, however, that full clinical validation of an mNGS assay is a substantial undertaking: rigorous determination of analytic sensitivity and specificity, limits of detection across organism classes, reproducibility, and the regulatory and qualitysystem requirements for a laboratory-developed test carry a cost and complexity that are themselves a major barrier. 22 A pragmatic near-term path is therefore to use mNGS as a research and epidemiologic surveillance tool -for example, in this study, the prevalence of T. gondii has raised interest in making a singleplex T. gondii PCR clinically available at HNDM.

A man aged 46-50 recently diagnosed with multiple myeloma presented with several days of new headache.
On admission, CSF analysis demonstrated pleocytosis (105 WBC/µL, 97% mononuclear and 3% neutrophils), elevated protein (97 mg/dL), and glucose 83 mg/dL.
MRI brain with and without contrast demonstrated a left temporal abscess with restricted diffusion and surrounding edema.
He underwent craniotomy with abscess drainage; subsequent abscess culture grew Listeria monocytogenes.
This pathogen was missed on both in-country shallowdepth mNGS and deep-sequencing.

Participants were enrolled at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo (HNDM), a large public hospital in central Lima, Peru, and the study protocol was approved by the institutional review boards of the University of California San Francisco (#24-41322), HNDM (Registro #27060, Código #8967), and Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia (UPCH, #197-17-25).
It is estimated that 300-400 patients are admitted annually with a suspected CNS infection, but fewer than 25% of patients receive a microbiologically confirmed diagnosis.

The hospital's available diagnostic testing for neurologic infections included Gram stain, bacterial/fungal/AFB culture, India ink staining, GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid), and FilmArray PCR (BioFire Diagnostics, includes Escherichia coli K1, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2), human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), enterovirus, human parechovirus, varicella zoster virus (VZV), and Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii).
Admitted adults who underwent lumbar puncture due to suspected CNS infection from August 2024 -April 2025 were screened for participation.
